name: BMP-assisted distraction

card.summary: Pairing bone morphogenetic protein with distraction osteogenesis (surgical bone lengthening) to speed new bone formation, which could shorten the time spent lengthening height or facial bone.
card.note: Experimental in lengthening; BMP products carry FDA-reported complications in other uses.

quick.overview:
Distraction osteogenesis is the surgical method behind limb lengthening and some jaw and midface advancement: a bone is cut and slowly pulled apart while new bone fills the gap. Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) are signalling proteins that stimulate bone formation, and researchers have explored adding them to lengthening to speed up the bone-filling phase.

The appeal for height and face-structure seekers is a shorter recovery with the device in place. The research is mostly in animals, with mixed results on whether BMP simply speeds healing or changes bone quality.
quick.how: In the research settings where it has been studied, BMP is delivered locally at the lengthening site, for example on a collagen carrier or by injection, alongside a standard distraction device. It is a surgeon-led, experimental add-on rather than something people do themselves; results are judged on bone strength and imaging after the consolidation period.
quick.risks: Distraction osteogenesis itself has reported infection, nonunion, hardware failure and nerve injury rates. BMP products approved for spinal and fracture use have documented complications, including swelling in cervical use, and an FDA notification on it. Use in limb or facial lengthening is off-label or experimental.

lead: BMP-assisted distraction refers to combining bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) with distraction osteogenesis, the technique in which a surgically cut bone is gradually separated so new bone forms in the gap.[1] The same principle underlies cosmetic and reconstructive limb lengthening and jaw or midface advancement.[1] The idea in appearance terms is a faster route to the added height or facial projection by shortening the consolidation period.

BMPs were named by Marshall Urist in 1971 after his 1965 finding that demineralised bone induced new bone formation.[2] Recombinant BMP-2 and BMP-7 are marketed on collagen carriers for spinal fusion and certain fracture uses.[2] Wikipedia notes that, as of 2013, researchers were exploring combining BMP with distraction devices.[1]
Published work on the combination is largely animal-based, including sheep tibial lengthening studies, and results have varied with carrier, dose and timing.

chain: BMP applied at the lengthening site
Faster or stronger new bone in the gap
Shorter consolidation and device time, more reliable gain
angle.text: The aim is to speed up or strengthen the bone that fills a surgical lengthening gap, so the height or facial advancement achieved by distraction is secured sooner. It is a research-stage adjunct to lengthening surgery.

paras: Distraction osteogenesis proceeds in phases: a bone cut, a latency period of about a week, gradual separation at roughly 1 mm per day, then a consolidation period while the bone hardens, followed by device removal.[1] Separating too fast risks nonunion, while too slow can let the bone fuse early.[1]
BMP-assisted approaches try to shorten or improve the consolidation phase by adding an osteoinductive protein locally.

Urist's 1965 rabbit experiments showed that demineralised freeze-dried bone induced new bone in muscle, and later work by Reddi and Sampath led to cloning of the BMPs.[2] Medtronic's BMP-2 product (INFUSE) was approved in 2002 for lumbar interbody fusion, with later approvals including open tibial fractures; Stryker's BMP-7 (OP-1) received humanitarian device exemptions in 2001 and 2004.[2] Both use a collagen matrix.[2]

No studies found. Related animal research: in a sheep study of 25 mm tibial lengthening, three local rhBMP-2 injections were associated with higher cortical bone fraction and several-fold higher torsional and bending stiffness at day 74 than no injection.[3] The authors noted microarchitecture was measured at a single time point.
Distraction osteogenesis complications reported include infection (about 5%), growth in an unintended direction (7-9%), hardware failure and, in mandibular cases, nerve injury.[1]

For BMP, a 2008 FDA notification concerned swelling and airway or swallowing complications in cervical fusion; early trials are described as having underreported adverse events, and up to 85% of use has been off-label.[2]

timeline.event: Codivilla publishes the first clinical attempt at limb lengthening.[1]
Urist shows demineralised bone induces new bone in rabbits.[2]
BMP-2 (INFUSE) approved for lumbar interbody fusion.[2]
Sheep study of repeated rhBMP-2 injections in tibial distraction published.[3]
